name: Motretinide
lead: Motretinide is an aromatic retinoid, an analogue of retinoic acid, classed as a topical anti-acne agent (ATC code D10AD05).[1][2] It has been described as a retinoid once used on the skin for acne; it is not among the retinoids in common use today.[1]

The published evidence is mostly from the 1980s: a comparison against benzoyl peroxide in acne vulgaris, animal assays of retinoid activity, and teratogenicity testing alongside other retinoids.[3][4][5] Discussion of it in looksmaxxing communities was not found in the available sources.
infobox: Not in common use; status not stated in sources

paras: Motretinide was developed as a topical treatment for acne, grouped by reference works with retinoids such as tretinoin, isotretinoin, adapalene and tazarotene.[1][2]

A 1984 report in Dermatologica compared motretinide with benzoyl peroxide in the treatment of acne vulgaris.[3] Only the title was available in the sources reviewed, so its results are not summarized here.

Motretinide was also included in a 1984 rhino-mouse assay of the antikeratinizing effects of retinoids, an animal model, in which it was compared with all-trans-retinoic acid, 13-cis-retinoic acid and etretinate.[4]

Retinoids act by binding nuclear retinoid receptors, and review literature describes them as relatively selective in targeting skin structures.[1] Methods papers from the 1980s used motretinide among compounds when developing ways to measure the activity of topically applied retinoids.[4][6]

Aromatic retinoids as a group have teratogenic potential. Motretinide was among the retinoids included in limb-bud cell culture work validating a teratogenicity screening system.[5] Transplacental studies in mice examined etretinate and other aromatic retinoids.[7]

card.summary: A largely historical topical acne retinoid with a 1984 trial against benzoyl peroxide and little modern literature.
card.note: Not in common use; retinoids as a class carry teratogenicity concerns.

quick.overview:
Motretinide is an older topical retinoid that was used for acne. Wikipedia describes it as an aromatic analogue of retinoic acid and a stub-level entry.

Most published work dates from the 1980s, including one comparison with benzoyl peroxide.
quick.mechanism: Like other retinoids it acts through nuclear retinoid receptors in skin cells, affecting keratinization; animal assays from the 1980s measured this antikeratinizing effect.
quick.risks: Aromatic retinoids as a class have teratogenic potential, and motretinide was included in teratogenicity screening work. Current regulatory and marketing status is not stated in the sources reviewed.
